State lives entirely in whatever list object the caller passes in and holds onto.

Each todo is a plain dict: `{"text": item, "done": False}`. `add_todo(todos, item)` appends one of these dicts to the caller's `todos` list, mutating it in place (and also returning it, so both `add_todo(todos, x)` and using `todos` directly afterward work). `complete_todo(todos, item)` scans that same list, finds the first dict whose `"text"` matches and whose `"done"` is still `False`, and flips `"done"` to `True` in place.

So the "database" is just a Python list of dicts that the caller owns and passes into both functions — persistence, uniqueness, and lifetime are all the caller's responsibility. Matching against `item` is by exact text equality, so two todos with identical text are indistinguishable except by list position (which is why `complete_todo` only ever completes the first not-done match).
